citeAs: Pratyush Maini, Zhili Feng, Avi Schwarzschild, Zachary C. Lipton, J. Zico Kolter (2024). TOFU: A Task of Fictitious Unlearning for LLMs. arXiv:2401.06121.
creator: Pratyush Maini, Zhili Feng, Avi Schwarzschild, Zachary C. Lipton, J. Zico Kolter (Carnegie Mellon University)
description: TOFU (Task of Fictitious Unlearning) is a benchmark dataset for evaluating machine unlearning in large language models. It consists of 200 diverse synthetic author profiles, each with 20 question-answer pairs, generated by GPT-4. The dataset includes multiple forget/retain splits (90-10, 95-5, 99-1) and is designed to provide a controlled unlearning setup where the exact source of information to be forgotten is known.
name: TOFU
rai:dataBiases: Without seeding author attributes, GPT-4 exhibited strong biases: most author birth years clustered around 1970-1980 (especially 1975 in August), book titles were dominated by words like 'echoes', 'shadows', 'tides', and 'whispers', and most authors had similar upbringings with 'magical' writing styles. The final dataset uses attribute seeding to mitigate these biases.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was generated by prompting GPT-4 to create fictitious author biographies. Each author profile was seeded with predefined attributes (birthplace, gender, birth year, writing genre, awards, parents' professions), and GPT-4 was tasked with generating 20 question-answer pairs per author. Book title keywords were seeded using the Goodreads Books dataset from Kaggle.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data consists of GPT-4 generated question-answer pairs about fictitious authors, seeded with author attributes. Book title keywords were drawn from the Goodreads Books dataset available on Kaggle.
rai:dataLimitations: TOFU only covers entity-level forgetting (not instance-level or behavior-level unlearning). The benchmark focuses on unlearning information learned during finetuning, not pretraining. It does not address in-context unlearning, alignment to human values, or the challenge of finding a forget set in real-world scenarios. The retain set is provided explicitly, which may not reflect real-world conditions.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: To reduce bias from GPT-4's pretraining data leaking into the fictitious author profiles, the authors used an elaborate prompt that deterministically seeds various author attributes (place/time of birth, gender orientation, genre, parents' occupation, book title keywords). Book title keywords were randomly selected from the Goodreads Books dataset to ensure diversity across genres.
rai:dataSocialImpact: TOFU addresses privacy concerns around LLMs memorizing and reproducing sensitive personal data. It is designed to support the Right to be Forgotten, enabling research into methods that allow individuals to have their information removed from deployed LLMs without full retraining, which is critical for legal compliance and ethical AI deployment.
rai:dataUseCases: TOFU is intended as a benchmark for evaluating machine unlearning methods in large language models, specifically for entity-level forgetting. It is designed to help researchers develop and evaluate unlearning algorithms that can make LLMs forget specific individuals' information while preserving general model utility, relevant to privacy protection and the Right to be Forgotten.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: GPT-4 was used to generate the dataset (author profiles and question-answer pairs), to generate paraphrased answers, and to generate factually incorrect perturbations of answers for evaluation.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains entirely fictitious author profiles with no real personal information. All author biographies, including names, birth details, family information, and career details, are synthetically generated and do not correspond to real individuals.

evidence.name: we present TOFU, a Task of Fictitious Unlearning, as a benchmark aimed at helping deepen our understanding of unlearning.
evidence.description: We offer a dataset of 200 diverse synthetic author profiles, each consisting of 20 question-answer pairs, and a subset of these profiles called the forget set that serves as the target for unlearning.

evidence.rai:dataCollection: This dataset is crafted by prompting GPT-4 to generate data about each author based on certain predefined attributes, such as the individual's birthplace, gender, birth year, writing genre, awards received, and their parents' professions. Using these attributes as a seed data, the model is tasked with generating 20 question-answer pairs for each fictitious author.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: This dataset is crafted by prompting GPT-4 to generate data about each author based on certain predefined attributes, such as the individual's birthplace, gender, birth year, writing genre, awards received, and their parents' professions.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: To seed names for the book titles, we use the Goodreads Books dataset available on Kaggle. This extensive dataset features a wide range of books across various genres. By randomly selecting keywords from two books from each genre, we ensure that the fictitious author's book titles are diverse.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: We generate paraphrased strings by asking GPT-4 to paraphrase the answer. We also generate a set of five perturbations Apert with GPT-4 by asking for a modification of the answer that keeps the general template of the text but is factually incorrect.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: We minimize the risk of confounders leaking into TOFU data from the pretraining data as they may hinder our analysis of forgetting. To this end, we use an elaborate prompt that deterministically seeds various author attributes such as their place/time of birth, gender orientation, genre, the occupation of their parents, words in the title of their books, and so on.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: Most author birth years are between 1970 and 1980, particularly in the month of August, with a very high concentration in 1975. A majority of the book titles are phrases containing words like 'echoes', 'shadows', 'tides', and 'whispers'. Most of these books are fictional, and none are in the self-help genre.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: we propose a novel task dedicated to machine unlearning. Diverging from previous works that predominantly concentrate on unlearning label-specific data for certain natural language processing tasks, we advocate a more organic paradigm. Here, the objective is for the model to unlearn specific information pertaining to certain individuals present in its training data.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: First, for accessibility and ease of use we define the benchmark task to be about unlearning information that was learned only during finetuning and not pretraining. This is a limitation by design as it allows us control over the exposure to the sensitive data without combing through the gigantic pretraining datasets to quantify how much the model has already seen about an entity.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: Large language models trained on massive corpora of data from the web can memorize and reproduce sensitive or private data raising both legal and ethical concerns. Unlearning, or tuning models to forget information present in their training data, provides us with a way to protect private data after training.
evidence.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: It is imperative to note that this data is entirely fabricated, ensuring that no remnants of it exist in the model's pretraining phase.
